output.briefing:
Work only on the assigned exceptional-anchor direction: the opposite-sign integer pair is {-1,1}. The supplied L1 proof establishes this reduction: if integer anchors have opposite signs, their product is an integer at most -1, and product plus 1 being a rational square forces the product to be at least -1. Hence the product is -1. For any other element x, 1+x and 1-x being squares imply -1≤x≤1; endpoints duplicate anchors, while the only integer strictly between them is zero, forbidden. Thus additional elements are noninteger rationals in (-1,1), not necessarily positive. The all-positive subcase cannot contain these anchors and is not resolved by this direction.

For an exact parameterization, write p²=1+x and q²=1-x. Then p²+q²=2 and x=p²-1. For any nonzero common neighbor, p≠1 (if p=1 then q=±1 and x=0), so the rational slope t=(q-1)/(p-1) is finite. Substitution of q=1+t(p-1) into the conic, taking the root other than the base point (1,1), gives
p=(t²-2t-1)/(t²+1), q=(1-2t-t²)/(t²+1), and x=f(t)=4t(1-t²)/(1+t²)².
Conversely these formulas satisfy p²+q²=2 and x=p²-1, so every rational t gives a common neighbor (possibly zero). The omitted conic point (1,1) and the other point with p=1, namely (1,-1), both correspond to x=0 and are irrelevant as tuple elements. This proves the parametrization for all nonzero rational common neighbors.

Define C={x∈Q:1+x and 1-x are rational squares}. A symmetric candidate {1,-1,u,-u,v,-v} is a D(1) sextuple exactly when u,v,uv∈C, u,v≠0, and u≠±v. Necessity follows from the anchor and cross-pairs. For sufficiency, these conditions give the anchor-to-element and cross-pair squares; the remaining pairs within opposite pairs have 1-u²=(1+u)(1-u) and 1-v²=(1+v)(1-v), also rational squares. These account for all fifteen pairs. Since ±1 are not in C, the only further collisions to check are precisely nonzero and u≠±v. Equivalently, set u=f(r), v=f(s), uv=f(w) for rational parameters and impose f(r)f(s)=f(w), together with those distinctness conditions. This is a correct algebraic reduction, but it is one relation in three parameters; it does not by itself produce a tractable curve or prove a rational-point obstruction.

For a contradiction-oriented continuation, study rational fibers of f(r)f(s)=f(w), separating exceptional and degenerate loci before attempting a descent or other global obstruction. Do not mistake this symmetric subfamily for the general exceptional-anchor case: a general sextuple containing {-1,1} requires four distinct common neighbors that are pairwise adjacent, with no opposite-pair symmetry assumed. No exact nondegenerate example or genuine obstruction is supplied here. Bounded searches cannot settle the rational-point question at unbounded height.

assumptions: All six elements belong to Q and are nonzero.
All six elements are pairwise distinct.
At least two elements belong to Z.
For each of the fifteen unordered pairs, the product plus 1 belongs to Q squared; a zero square root is allowed.
quantifiers: Existentially over six pairwise distinct nonzero rational numbers.
At least two of those six numbers are integers.
Universally over all fifteen unordered pairs.
Any nonexistence conclusion must cover unbounded rational height and every allowable integer pair.
problem_contract.statement: Determine whether there exists a set S of six pairwise distinct nonzero rational numbers such that at least two elements are integers and xy+1 is a rational square for every two distinct x,y in S. Track the all-positive case separately from the unrestricted-sign case. Give an exact valid example or an unrestricted nonexistence proof; otherwise record only explicitly scoped partial results.
